subject: Architecture
title: One Central Park: The Solar Mirror
description: A short lesson to help you apply One Central Park: The Solar Mirror.

hook.text: A Sydney apartment tower uses a giant motorized mirror to bounce sunlight into a shaded park below.

buildup.text: One Central Park's cantilever holds a heliostat — a mirror that tracks the sun across the sky.

discovery.text: The reflected light illuminates the park and lower apartments that would otherwise sit in shadow all day.

twist.text: Climbing plants cover 50% of the facade. An automated irrigation system waters them using recycled water.

climax.text: The building has its own water recycling plant that processes blackwater for toilet flushing and irrigation.

punchline.text: A mirror, a garden, and a water plant. All on one apartment building.

quiz.question: What does the heliostat on One Central Park do?
options: Bounces sunlight into shaded areas below the building
Blocks glare from entering apartment windows

details.summary: One Central Park in Sydney uses a motorized heliostat — a large reflector mounted on a cantilever arm — to redirect sunlight into the shaded park below and onto lower building facades.
details.whyItMatters: One Central Park solves a common urban problem — tall buildings casting shadows — with an inventive engineering response. The heliostat redirects sunlight that the building steals.
takeaways: A motorized heliostat redirects sunlight to shaded areas below
Climbing plants by Patrick Blanc cover extensive facade areas
It demonstrates that towers needn't permanently darken public spaces

faq.question: How does the heliostat work?
faq.answer: A large array of motorized mirrors mounted on a cantilevered arm tracks the sun and reflects light downward into the park and living spaces that the tower shadows. The mirrors adjust throughout the day to maintain optimal light redirection as the sun moves across the sky.

faq.question: How are the vertical gardens maintained?
faq.answer: An automated irrigation system delivers water and nutrients to each planting zone. Hydroponics support plants on the facade without heavy soil. Botanist Patrick Blanc selected species adapted to each facade's specific light, wind, and moisture conditions.
